entities.summary: François Guillaume de Castelnau de Clermont-Lodève (1480–1541) was a French diplomat and Cardinal. He was the son of Pierre-Tristan, Seigneur de Clermont et de Clermont-Lodève and Vicomte de Nébouzan, and Catherine d'Amboise. His father was a member of the Order of Saint Michael. François' grandmother had been heiress of Dieudonné Guillaume de Clermont. He had an elder brother, Pierre de Castelnau, who was heir to the family estates. François was also the nephew of Cardinal Georges d'Amboise (1498-1510), who was largely responsible for François' swift rise to prominence in the Church.

entities.name: François Guillaume de Castelnau-Clermont-Ludève
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
François Guillaume de Castelnau de Clermont-Lodève (c. 1480–1541) was a French Cardinal and diplomat who served as a key ecclesiastical agent of the French monarchy during the Italian Wars and the opening decades of the Protestant Reformation.

Born into minor Gascon nobility, he was the nephew of Cardinal Georges d'Amboise (1460–1510), Archbishop of Rouen and chief minister of Louis XII — a connection that catapulted his ecclesiastical career. By 1505 he held multiple benefices; by 1516 he was Bishop of Lodève in Languedoc under Francis I. He served on diplomatic missions to Rome and the imperial courts, navigating the complex terrain in which France sought papal alliance while simultaneously competing with the Habsburgs for Italian dominance.

His significance lies at the intersection of French royal patronage, the Counter-Reformation Church, and the fracturing Christian world of the 1520s–1540s. Pope Paul III created him Cardinal in 1538, late in his career — a recognition of his decades of service to both Crown and Church. As a product of the Amboise network and of Francoist ecclesiastical policy, he participated in negotiations through which France maintained its 'Most Christian King' status while forming the French-Ottoman alliance against Charles V. He died in 1541, representative of the generation of French clerics who administered the Church of France through the twin crises of Italian Wars and Reformation without abandoning either crown or tiara.
